# Deserialize in serde_core::de - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.226/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html

`pub trait Deserialize<'de>: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [deserialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.deserialize)<D>(deserializer: D) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, D::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where D: [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)<'de>;
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be deserialized from any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Deserialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/index.html). All of these
can be deserialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called `serde_derive` to
automatically generate `Deserialize` implementations for structs and enums
in your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html) for how to
use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Deserialize` manually for
some type in your program. See the [Implementing
 Deserialize](https://serde.rs/impl-deserialize.html) section of the manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Deserialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the `linked-hash-map` crate provides a
`LinkedHashMap<K, V>` type that is deserializable by Serde because the crate
provides an implementation of `Deserialize` for it.

[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
borrowed by `Self` when deserialized. See the page [Understanding
deserializer lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html) for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety", so this trait is not object safe.*

# Serialize in serde_core::ser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.226/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html

```
pub trait Serialize {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[serialize](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serialize)<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/result/enum.Result.html)<S::[Ok](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), S::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where S: [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html);
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be serialized into any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Serialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://docs.rs/index.html). All of
these can be serialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [ serde_derive](https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive) to
automatically generate

`Serialize` implementations for structs and enums in
your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html)for how to use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Serialize` manually for some
type in your program. See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the
manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Serialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the [ linked-hash-map](https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map) crate provides a

[type that is serializable by Serde because the crate provides an implementation of](https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html)

`LinkedHashMap<K, V>``Serialize` for it.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Serialize this value into the given Serde serializer.

See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the manual for more
information about how to implement this method.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
// This is what #[derive(Serialize)] would generate.
impl Serialize for Person {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut s = serializer.serialize_struct("Person", 3)?;
        s.serialize_field("name", &self.name)?;
        s.serialize_field("age", &self.age)?;
        s.serialize_field("phones", &self.phones)?;
        s.end()
    }
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety", so this trait is not object safe.*

# crossterm_keybind - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crossterm-keybind/0.4.3/crossterm_keybind/

## Expand description

This crate help you build tui with keybings config in an easy way. When building a tui application, we need address following topics.

- `Define a set of keybing for some events`
- `Capture one/some key bindings and perform one the event`
- `Display a prompt of a key bindings`
- `Provide a config file and let user to change all or part of it`

These topics can be abstract these into [ KeyBindTrait](https://docs.rs/trait.KeyBindTrait.html), and the key binding serialize and deserialize
to a config file are solved in this crate.

There still are a lot of trivial works, ahead you and your great ideal to build tui application.
This crate also provides derive macro [KeyBind](https://docs.rs/crossterm-keybind-derive/latest/crossterm_keybind_derive/derive.KeyBind.html)
to generate the the keyconfig in a supper easy way, you can have a toml key config for your
events and allow user to patch part of it.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [struct_patch](https://docs.rs/struct-patch/0.12.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/struct_patch/index.html);

# tanzim - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tanzim/0.13.0/tanzim/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#tanzim)tanzim

[ Package](https://crates.io/crates/tanzim)   |

[|](https://docs.rs/tanzim)

**Documentation**

**Repository**Facade crate for a small, composable configuration pipeline: **load → parse → merge**.

`tanzim` lets you describe *where* configuration comes from with short source
strings (environment variables, files, HTTP, …), parse each source into a
typed value tree that remembers its origin, and merge everything into one map
keyed by entry name. Every value keeps its source location, so errors point at
the exact file, line, and column.

[§](https://docs.rs#pipeline)Pipeline

```
"env(prefix=APP_)"  "file:/etc/app"          ← source strings
        │
        ▼  load     Load::load(source)            → Vec<Payload>      (raw bytes + maybe name + maybe format)
        ▼  parse    Parse::parse(bytes)      → LocatedValue      (typed tree + Location)
        ▼  merge    Merge::merge(parsed)           → HashMap<name, …>  (grouped + combined)
        │
        ▼
   merged configuration
```
`PipelineMulti::run()` (or `PipelineSingle::run()` for a unified value) executes all stages. Each stage is also callable on its
own via `load()`, `parse()`, and `merge()` — useful for
inspecting intermediate results or building a custom pipeline.

[§](https://docs.rs#workspace-crates)Workspace crates

`tanzim` re-exports each stage so you rarely depend on them directly, but they
are independently usable:

| Re-export | Crate | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| `source` | `tanzim-source` | Parse the `SOURCE[(OPTIONS)][?][:RESOURCE]`source-string format into a validated`Source` |
| `loader` | `tanzim-load` | `Load`trait +`env`/`file`/`http`/`closure`loaders →`Payload` |
| `parser` | `tanzim-parse` | `Parse`trait +`env`/`json`/`yaml`/`toml`parsers →`LocatedValue` |
| `merge` | `tanzim-merge` | `Merge`trait +`LastWins`/`DeepMerge`strategies → grouped map |
| — | `tanzim-value` | Core `Value`,`LocatedValue`,`Map`,`Location`,`Error`types shared by every stage |

[§](https://docs.rs#key-concepts)Key concepts

- **Source strings**use the- `tanzim-source`- `SOURCE [(OPTIONS)] [?] [:RESOURCE]`, e.g.- `env(prefix=APP_)`,- `file?:.env`.
- **Named entries**— each- `Payload`carries an optional- `maybe_name`. The merger groups by name; unnamed payloads (- `maybe_name == None`) all share the- `None`key.
- **Format auto-detection**— if a payload has no- `maybe_format`, parsers are probed via- `is_format_supported`; otherwise the format hint selects the parser.
- `ignore_errors`(- `?`)- `?`swallow load/parse failures silently instead of aborting the pipeline.
- **Located errors**— [- `Error`] renders one line by default; use- `{error:#}`for a source snippet with a caret underline.
- **Result aliases**—- `parse()`returns- `Vec<Parsed>`and- `merge()`/- `run()`return- `Merged`(- `HashMap<Option<String>, (Vec<Payload>, LocatedValue)>`).

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

| Feature | Enables |
|---|---|
| `load-env`/`load-file`/`load-http` | env / filesystem / HTTP (closure-based) loaders |
| `parse-env` | env parser |
| `parse-json`/`parse-yaml`/`parse-toml` | format parsers |
| `validate-default` | the std-only validators (no extra dependencies) |
| `validate-schema` | schema machinery ( `with_schema`, the validation stage) |
| `validate-<name>` | one validator (e.g. `validate-url`,`validate-regex`), pulling in`validate-schema` |
| `validate-full` | every validator + schema |
| `full` | all loaders + all parsers + `validate-full`(examples, smoke test) |
| `logging`/`tracing` | optional log integration across all crates |

Defaults: `load-env`, `load-file`, `load-http`, `parse-env`, `validate-default`, `validate-schema`.

Use individual workspace crates if you only need one stage — see [tanzim-load/README.md](https://docs.rs/crates/tanzim-load/README.md), [tanzim-parse/README.md](https://docs.rs/crates/tanzim-parse/README.md), [tanzim-merge/README.md](https://docs.rs/crates/tanzim-merge/README.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use tanzim::multi::PipelineMultiBuilder;
use tanzim::loader::{env::Env, file::File};
use tanzim::parser::{env::Env as EnvParser, json::Json, yaml::Yaml, toml::Toml};
use tanzim::merge::DeepMerge;
fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let merged = PipelineMultiBuilder::new()
        .with_loader(Env::new())
        .with_loader(File::new())
        .with_parser(EnvParser::new())
        .with_parser(Json::new())
        .with_parser(Yaml::new())
        .with_parser(Toml::new())
        .with_merger(DeepMerge)
        .with_source("env(prefix=MY_APP_,separator=.)")?
        .with_source("file:examples/full/etc")?
        .build()?
        .run()?;
    for (name, (_sources, value)) in &merged {
        let display = match name {
            None => "(unnamed)",
            Some(n) => n.as_str(),
        };
        println!("{display}: {value}");
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
make examples        # run every example
make example-full    # full pipeline over env + file sources
```
`example-full` reads the source strings declared in the `Makefile` and the
sample config under `examples/full/etc/`. The individual stage crates ship their
own examples too (see each crate’s `examples/` directory).

[§](https://docs.rs#development)Development

```
make all          # build every crate
make test         # run unit tests + doctests across the workspace
make clippy       # lint with `-D warnings` across all targets and features
make check-style  # cargo fmt --check
make docs         # build rustdoc for the whole workspace
```

# tanzim_merge - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tanzim-merge/0.8.0/tanzim_merge/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#tanzim-merge)tanzim-merge

Third stage of the tanzim pipeline: groups parsed payloads by entry name and merges their values.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-merge-trait)The `Merge` trait

Implement [ Merge](https://docs.rs/trait.Merge.html) to define a custom merge strategy. The output is

[— a](https://docs.rs/type.Merged.html)

`Merged``HashMap<Option<String>, (Vec<Payload>, LocatedValue)>` keyed by entry
name, where the `Vec<Payload>` records which payloads contributed to each merged
value.[§](https://docs.rs#grouping-key)Grouping key

`Payload::maybe_name` determines the map key:

- `Some("foo")`→ key- `Some("foo")`
- `None`→ key- `None`(all unnamed payloads share this bucket)

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-strategies)Built-in strategies

| Type | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `LastWins` | Last value for each name fully replaces any previous value |
| `DeepMerge` | Maps are merged recursively; the overlay value wins at each non-map leaf |

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use tanzim_merge::{DeepMerge, LastWins, Merge};
use tanzim_load::Payload;
use tanzim_source::Source;
use tanzim_value::{LocatedValue, Location, Map, Value};
let source = Source::parse("env").unwrap();
let make_entry = |name: Option<&str>, key: &str, val: &str| {
    let loc = Location::at("env", "", None, None, None);
    let mut map = Map::new();
    map.insert(key.to_string(), LocatedValue { value: Value::String(val.to_string()), location: loc.clone() });
    let payload = Payload {
        source: source.clone(),
        maybe_name: name.map(str::to_string),
        maybe_format: Some("env".into()),
        content: vec![],
    };
    (payload, LocatedValue { value: Value::Map(map), location: loc })
};
let list = vec![
    make_entry(Some("db"), "host", "primary"),
    make_entry(Some("db"), "host", "replica"),
];
// LastWins: second entry fully replaces the first
let merged = LastWins.merge(&list).unwrap();
let db = merged.get(&Some("db".to_string())).unwrap();
let host = db.1.value.as_map().unwrap().get("host").unwrap();
assert_eq!(host.value.as_string().unwrap(), "replica");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

No default features. Opt-in `logging` / `tracing` emit log messages / trace
spans via the `log` / `tracing` crates.

[§](https://docs.rs#relations)Relations

- Consumes `LocatedValue`from`tanzim-parse`
- Uses `Payload`from`tanzim-load``Source`) to track provenance.
- Full pipeline wired in `tanzim`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Deep](https://docs.rs/struct.DeepMerge.html)- Merge
- Deep-merge merger: maps with the same name are merged recursively.
- [Last](https://docs.rs/struct.LastWins.html)- Wins
- Last-write-wins merger: each name keeps only its last-seen value.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Merge error type.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Merge](https://docs.rs/trait.Merge.html)
- Merges parsed payloads grouped by entry name.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Merged](https://docs.rs/type.Merged.html)
- Merge result: entry name → (contributing payloads, merged value).

# sim_lib_discrete_rank - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-discrete-rank/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_discrete_rank/

## Expand description

Discrete rank adapters.

This is the only discrete crate allowed to depend on `sim-lib-rank`. It hosts finite
rank spaces (bit-vector, subset, combination, permutation, simple-graph,
FWHT-signal), rank metrics, and grade compilers that synthesize a rank grade
from algebraic / spectral invariants (MST weight, closure density, Walsh
spectral entropy).

Boundary: `sim-lib-rank` must never depend on this crate; the dependency is
one-way.

- `pub use combinatorial::`- [CombinationSpace](https://docs.rs/combinatorial/struct.CombinationSpace.html);
- `pub use combinatorial::`- [PermutationSpace](https://docs.rs/combinatorial/struct.PermutationSpace.html);
- `pub use descriptor::`- [CardSpec](https://docs.rs/descriptor/struct.CardSpec.html);
- `pub use descriptor::`- [SpaceDescriptor](https://docs.rs/descriptor/struct.SpaceDescriptor.html);
- `pub use error::`- [RankAdapterError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.RankAdapterError.html);
- `pub use grade::`- [closure_density_grade](https://docs.rs/grade/fn.closure_density_grade.html);
- `pub use grade::`- [mst_weight_grade](https://docs.rs/grade/fn.mst_weight_grade.html);
- `pub use grade::`- [signal_spectral_entropy_grade](https://docs.rs/grade/fn.signal_spectral_entropy_grade.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [cards](https://docs.rs/cards/index.html)
- Card content for the discrete rank spaces. The facade install turns these
into kernel claims via `publish_space_claims`(which needs a`Cx`).

- Combination, permutation, and bounded-integer-vector rank spaces.

- Error type for the discrete rank adapters.

- [lattice](https://docs.rs/lattice/index.html)
- Bit-vector and subset rank spaces (bitmask order).
- [metric](https://docs.rs/metric/index.html)
- Nat-valued distance helpers for the discrete rank spaces.

# serde_with 3.21.0 - Docs.rs

# Custom de/serialization functions for Rust's [serde](https://serde.rs)

This crate provides custom de/serialization helpers to use in combination with [serde's  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with) and with the improved

[-annotation. Some common use cases are:](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/serde_as/index.html)

`serde_as`- De/Serializing a type using the `Display`and`FromStr`traits, e.g., for`u8`,`url::Url`, or`mime::Mime`. Check`DisplayFromStr`
- Support for arrays larger than 32 elements or using const generics.
With `serde_as`large arrays are supported, even if they are nested in other types.`[bool; 64]`,`Option<[u8; M]>`, and`Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>`are all supported, as[this examples shows](https://docs.rs#large-and-const-generic-arrays).
- Skip serializing all empty `Option`types with`#[skip_serializing_none]`
- Apply a prefix / suffix to each field name of a struct, without changing the de/serialize implementations of the struct using `with_prefix!``with_suffix!`
- Deserialize a comma separated list like `#hash,#tags,#are,#great`into a`Vec<String>`. Check the documentation for`serde_with::StringWithSeparator::<CommaSeparator, T>`

### Getting Help

**Check out the  user guide to find out more tips and tricks about this crate.**

For further help using this crate, you can [open a new discussion](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/discussions/new) or ask on [users.rust-lang.org](https://users.rust-lang.org/).
For bugs, please open a [new issue](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/issues/new) on GitHub.

## Use `serde_with` in your Project

```
# Add the current version to your Cargo.toml
```
The crate contains different features for integration with other common crates.
Check the [feature flags](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/feature_flags/index.html) section for information about all available features.

## Examples

Annotate your struct or enum to enable the custom de/serializer.
The `#[serde_as]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

The `as` is analogous to the `with` attribute of serde.
You mirror the type structure of the field you want to de/serialize.
You can specify converters for the inner types of a field, e.g., `Vec<DisplayFromStr>`.
The default de/serialization behavior can be restored by using `_` as a placeholder, e.g., `BTreeMap<_, DisplayFromStr>`.

`DisplayFromStr`

```
// This will serialize
Foo
// into this JSON
```
### Large and const-generic arrays

serde does not support arrays with more than 32 elements or using const-generics.
The `serde_as` attribute allows circumventing this restriction, even for nested types and nested arrays.

On top of it, `[u8; N]` (aka, bytes) can use the specialized `"Bytes"` for efficiency much like the `serde_bytes` crate.

```
// This allows us to serialize a struct like this
let arrays:  = Arrays ;
assert!;
```
`skip_serializing_none`

This situation often occurs with JSON, but other formats also support optional fields.
If many fields are optional, putting the annotations on the structs can become tedious.
The `#[skip_serializing_none]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

```
// This will serialize
Foo
// into this JSON
```
### Advanced `serde_as` usage

This example is mainly supposed to highlight the flexibility of the `serde_as` annotation compared to [serde's  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with).
More details about

`serde_as` can be found in the [user guide](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/index.html).

```
use Duration;
// This will serialize
Durations
// into this JSON
// and serializes
Bytes
// into this JSON
```

# serde_with - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/serde_with/3.21.0/target-redirect/serde_with/

## Expand description

This crate provides custom de/serialization helpers to use in combination with [serde’s  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with) and with the improved

[-annotation. Some common use cases are:](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/serde_as/index.html)

`serde_as`- De/Serializing a type using the `Display`and`FromStr`traits, e.g., for`u8`,`url::Url`, or`mime::Mime`. Check`DisplayFromStr`
- Support for arrays larger than 32 elements or using const generics.
With `serde_as`large arrays are supported, even if they are nested in other types.`[bool; 64]`,`Option<[u8; M]>`, and`Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>`are all supported, as[this examples shows](https://docs.rs#large-and-const-generic-arrays).
- Skip serializing all empty `Option`types with`#[skip_serializing_none]`
- Apply a prefix / suffix to each field name of a struct, without changing the de/serialize implementations of the struct using `with_prefix!``with_suffix!`
- Deserialize a comma separated list like `#hash,#tags,#are,#great`into a`Vec<String>`. Check the documentation for`serde_with::StringWithSeparator::<CommaSeparator, T>`

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-help)Getting Help

**Check out the  user guide to find out more tips and tricks about this crate.**

For further help using this crate you can [open a new discussion](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/discussions/new) or ask on [users.rust-lang.org](https://users.rust-lang.org/).
For bugs, please open a [new issue](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/issues/new) on GitHub.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-serde_with-in-your-project)Use `serde_with` in your Project

```
# Add the current version to your Cargo.toml
cargo add serde_with
```
The crate contains different features for integration with other common crates.
Check the [feature flags](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/feature_flags/index.html) section for information about all available features.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Annotate your struct or enum to enable the custom de/serializer.
The `#[serde_as]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

The `as` is analogous to the `with` attribute of serde.
You mirror the type structure of the field you want to de/serialize.
You can specify converters for the inner types of a field, e.g., `Vec<DisplayFromStr>`.
The default de/serialization behavior can be restored by using `_` as a placeholder, e.g., `BTreeMap<_, DisplayFromStr>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#displayfromstr)`DisplayFromStr`

```
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Foo {
    // Serialize with Display, deserialize with FromStr
    #[serde_as(as = "DisplayFromStr")]
    bar: u8,
}
// This will serialize
Foo {bar: 12}
// into this JSON
{"bar": "12"}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#large-and-const-generic-arrays)Large and const-generic arrays

serde does not support arrays with more than 32 elements or using const-generics.
The `serde_as` attribute allows circumventing this restriction, even for nested types and nested arrays.

On top of it, `[u8; N]` (aka, bytes) can use the specialized `"Bytes"` for efficiency much like the `serde_bytes` crate.

```
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Arrays<const N: usize, const M: usize> {
    #[serde_as(as = "[_; N]")]
    constgeneric: [bool; N],
    #[serde_as(as = "Box<[[_; 64]; N]>")]
    nested: Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>,
    #[serde_as(as = "Option<[_; M]>")]
    optional: Option<[u8; M]>,
    #[serde_as(as = "Bytes")]
    bytes: [u8; M],
}
// This allows us to serialize a struct like this
let arrays: Arrays<100, 128> = Arrays {
    constgeneric: [true; 100],
    nested: Box::new([[111; 64]; 100]),
    optional: Some([222; 128]),
    bytes: [0x42; 128],
};
assert!(serde_json::to_string(&arrays).is_ok());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#skip_serializing_none)`skip_serializing_none`

This situation often occurs with JSON, but other formats also support optional fields.
If many fields are optional, putting the annotations on the structs can become tedious.
The `#[skip_serializing_none]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

```
#[skip_serializing_none]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Foo {
    a: Option<usize>,
    b: Option<usize>,
    c: Option<usize>,
    d: Option<usize>,
    e: Option<usize>,
    f: Option<usize>,
    g: Option<usize>,
}
// This will serialize
Foo {a: None, b: None, c: None, d: Some(4), e: None, f: None, g: Some(7)}
// into this JSON
{"d": 4, "g": 7}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-serde_as-usage)Advanced `serde_as` usage

This example is mainly supposed to highlight the flexibility of the `serde_as` annotation compared to [serde’s  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with).
More details about

`serde_as` can be found in the [user guide](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/index.html).

```
use std::time::Duration;
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
enum Foo {
    Durations(
        // Serialize them into a list of number as seconds
        #[serde_as(as = "Vec<DurationSeconds>")]
        Vec<Duration>,
    ),
    Bytes {
        // We can treat a Vec like a map with duplicates.
        // JSON only allows string keys, so convert i32 to strings
        // The bytes will be hex encoded
        #[serde_as(as = "Map<DisplayFromStr, Hex>")]
        bytes: Vec<(i32, Vec<u8>)>,
    }
}
// This will serialize
Foo::Durations(
    vec![Duration::new(5, 0), Duration::new(3600, 0), Duration::new(0, 0)]
)
// into this JSON
{
    "Durations": [5, 3600, 0]
}
// and serializes
Foo::Bytes {
    bytes: vec![
        (1, vec![0, 1, 2]),
        (-100, vec![100, 200, 255]),
        (1, vec![0, 111, 222]),
    ],
}
// into this JSON
{
    "Bytes": {
        "bytes": {
            "1": "000102",
            "-100": "64c8ff",
            "1": "006fde"
        }
    }
}
```

# serde_with - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/index.html

## Expand description

This crate provides custom de/serialization helpers to use in combination with [serde’s  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with) and with the improved

[-annotation. Some common use cases are:](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/serde_as/index.html)

`serde_as`- De/Serializing a type using the `Display`and`FromStr`traits, e.g., for`u8`,`url::Url`, or`mime::Mime`. Check`DisplayFromStr`
- Support for arrays larger than 32 elements or using const generics.
With `serde_as`large arrays are supported, even if they are nested in other types.`[bool; 64]`,`Option<[u8; M]>`, and`Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>`are all supported, as[this examples shows](https://docs.rs#large-and-const-generic-arrays).
- Skip serializing all empty `Option`types with`#[skip_serializing_none]`
- Apply a prefix / suffix to each field name of a struct, without changing the de/serialize implementations of the struct using `with_prefix!``with_suffix!`
- Deserialize a comma separated list like `#hash,#tags,#are,#great`into a`Vec<String>`. Check the documentation for`serde_with::StringWithSeparator::<CommaSeparator, T>`

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-help)Getting Help

**Check out the  user guide to find out more tips and tricks about this crate.**

For further help using this crate you can [open a new discussion](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/discussions/new) or ask on [users.rust-lang.org](https://users.rust-lang.org/).
For bugs, please open a [new issue](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/issues/new) on GitHub.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-serde_with-in-your-project)Use `serde_with` in your Project

```
# Add the current version to your Cargo.toml
cargo add serde_with
```
The crate contains different features for integration with other common crates.
Check the [feature flags](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/feature_flags/index.html) section for information about all available features.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Annotate your struct or enum to enable the custom de/serializer.
The `#[serde_as]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

The `as` is analogous to the `with` attribute of serde.
You mirror the type structure of the field you want to de/serialize.
You can specify converters for the inner types of a field, e.g., `Vec<DisplayFromStr>`.
The default de/serialization behavior can be restored by using `_` as a placeholder, e.g., `BTreeMap<_, DisplayFromStr>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#displayfromstr)`DisplayFromStr`

```
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Foo {
    // Serialize with Display, deserialize with FromStr
    #[serde_as(as = "DisplayFromStr")]
    bar: u8,
}
// This will serialize
Foo {bar: 12}
// into this JSON
{"bar": "12"}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#large-and-const-generic-arrays)Large and const-generic arrays

serde does not support arrays with more than 32 elements or using const-generics.
The `serde_as` attribute allows circumventing this restriction, even for nested types and nested arrays.

On top of it, `[u8; N]` (aka, bytes) can use the specialized `"Bytes"` for efficiency much like the `serde_bytes` crate.

```
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Arrays<const N: usize, const M: usize> {
    #[serde_as(as = "[_; N]")]
    constgeneric: [bool; N],
    #[serde_as(as = "Box<[[_; 64]; N]>")]
    nested: Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>,
    #[serde_as(as = "Option<[_; M]>")]
    optional: Option<[u8; M]>,
    #[serde_as(as = "Bytes")]
    bytes: [u8; M],
}
// This allows us to serialize a struct like this
let arrays: Arrays<100, 128> = Arrays {
    constgeneric: [true; 100],
    nested: Box::new([[111; 64]; 100]),
    optional: Some([222; 128]),
    bytes: [0x42; 128],
};
assert!(serde_json::to_string(&arrays).is_ok());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#skip_serializing_none)`skip_serializing_none`

This situation often occurs with JSON, but other formats also support optional fields.
If many fields are optional, putting the annotations on the structs can become tedious.
The `#[skip_serializing_none]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

```
#[skip_serializing_none]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Foo {
    a: Option<usize>,
    b: Option<usize>,
    c: Option<usize>,
    d: Option<usize>,
    e: Option<usize>,
    f: Option<usize>,
    g: Option<usize>,
}
// This will serialize
Foo {a: None, b: None, c: None, d: Some(4), e: None, f: None, g: Some(7)}
// into this JSON
{"d": 4, "g": 7}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-serde_as-usage)Advanced `serde_as` usage

This example is mainly supposed to highlight the flexibility of the `serde_as` annotation compared to [serde’s  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with).
More details about

`serde_as` can be found in the [user guide](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/index.html).

```
use std::time::Duration;
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
enum Foo {
    Durations(
        // Serialize them into a list of number as seconds
        #[serde_as(as = "Vec<DurationSeconds>")]
        Vec<Duration>,
    ),
    Bytes {
        // We can treat a Vec like a map with duplicates.
        // JSON only allows string keys, so convert i32 to strings
        // The bytes will be hex encoded
        #[serde_as(as = "Map<DisplayFromStr, Hex>")]
        bytes: Vec<(i32, Vec<u8>)>,
    }
}
// This will serialize
Foo::Durations(
    vec![Duration::new(5, 0), Duration::new(3600, 0), Duration::new(0, 0)]
)
// into this JSON
{
    "Durations": [5, 3600, 0]
}
// and serializes
Foo::Bytes {
    bytes: vec![
        (1, vec![0, 1, 2]),
        (-100, vec![100, 200, 255]),
        (1, vec![0, 111, 222]),
    ],
}
// into this JSON
{
    "Bytes": {
        "bytes": {
            "1": "000102",
            "-100": "64c8ff",
            "1": "006fde"
        }
    }
}
```

- [Same](https://docs.rs/struct.Same.html)
- Adapter to convert from `serde_as`to the serde traits.
- [Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.Schema.html)- `schemars_0_8`or- `schemars_0_9`or- `schemars_1`
- Helper for implementing `JsonSchema`
- [Seq](https://docs.rs/struct.Seq.html)
- De/Serialize a Map into a list of tuples
- [SetLast](https://docs.rs/struct.SetLastValueWins.html)- Value - Wins - `alloc`
- Ensure that the last value is taken, if duplicate values exist
- [SetPrevent](https://docs.rs/struct.SetPreventDuplicates.html)- Duplicates - `alloc`
- Ensure no duplicate values exist in a set.
- [String](https://docs.rs/struct.StringWithSeparator.html)- With - Separator
- De/Serialize a delimited collection using `Display``FromStr`
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.TimestampMicroSeconds.html)- Micro - Seconds
- Equivalent to `TimestampSeconds`
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.TimestampMicroSecondsWithFrac.html)- Micro - Seconds - With - Frac
- Equivalent to `TimestampSecondsWithFrac`
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.TimestampMilliSeconds.html)- Milli - Seconds
- Equivalent to `TimestampSeconds`
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.TimestampMilliSecondsWithFrac.html)- Milli - Seconds - With - Frac
- Equivalent to `TimestampSecondsWithFrac`
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.TimestampNanoSeconds.html)- Nano - Seconds
- Equivalent to `TimestampSeconds`
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.TimestampNanoSecondsWithFrac.html)- Nano - Seconds - With - Frac
- Equivalent to `TimestampSecondsWithFrac`
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.TimestampSeconds.html)- Seconds
- De/Serialize timestamps as seconds since the UNIX epoch
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.TimestampSecondsWithFrac.html)- Seconds - With - Frac
- De/Serialize timestamps as seconds since the UNIX epoch
- [TryFrom](https://docs.rs/struct.TryFromInto.html)- Into
- Serialize value by converting to/from a proxy type with serde support.
- [TryFrom](https://docs.rs/struct.TryFromIntoRef.html)- Into - Ref
- Serialize a reference value by converting to/from a proxy type with serde support.
- [VecSkip](https://docs.rs/struct.VecSkipError.html)- Error - `alloc`
- Deserialize a sequence into `Vec<T>`, skipping elements which fail to deserialize.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.DeserializeAs.html)- As
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde, analogue to`Deserialize`
- [Inspect](https://docs.rs/trait.InspectError.html)- Error - `alloc`
- A trait to inspect skipped deserialization errors
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.SerializeAs.html)- As
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde, analogue to`Serialize`

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [apply](https://docs.rs/attr.apply.html)- `macros`
- Apply attributes to all fields with matching types
- [serde_](https://docs.rs/attr.serde_as.html)- as - `macros`
- Convenience macro to use the `serde_as`
- [skip_](https://docs.rs/attr.skip_serializing_none.html)- serializing_ - none - `macros`
- Add `skip_serializing_if`annotations to [`Option`] fields.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.DeserializeFromStr.html)- From - Str - `macros`
- Deserialize value by using its `FromStr`
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.SerializeDisplay.html)- Display - `macros`
- Serialize value by using it’s `Display`
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.SerializeDisplayAlt.html)- Display - Alt - `macros`
- Serialize value by using its `Display``#`) format flag

[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! [![crates.io badge](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/serde_with.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/serde_with/)
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! [![Build Status](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/actions/workflows/ci.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with)
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! [![codecov](https://codecov.io/gh/jonasbb/serde_with/branch/master/graph/badge.svg)](https://codecov.io/gh/jonasbb/serde_with)
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! [![CII Best Practices](https://bestpractices.coreinfrastructure.org/projects/4322/badge)](https://bestpractices.coreinfrastructure.org/projects/4322)
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! ---
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! This crate provides custom de/serialization helpers to use in combination with [serde's `with` annotation][with-annotation] and with the improved [`serde_as`][as-annotation]-annotation.
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! Some common use cases are:
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! * De/Serializing a type using the `Display` and `FromStr` traits, e.g., for `u8`, `url::Url`, or `mime::Mime`.
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!   Check [`DisplayFromStr`] for details.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! * Support for arrays larger than 32 elements or using const generics.
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!   With `serde_as` large arrays are supported, even if they are nested in other types.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!   `[bool; 64]`, `Option<[u8; M]>`, and `Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>` are all supported, as [this examples shows](#large-and-const-generic-arrays).
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! * Skip serializing all empty `Option` types with [`#[skip_serializing_none]`][skip_serializing_none].
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! * Apply a prefix / suffix to each field name of a struct, without changing the de/serialize implementations of the struct using [`with_prefix!`][] / [`with_suffix!`][].
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! * Deserialize a comma separated list like `#hash,#tags,#are,#great` into a `Vec<String>`.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!   Check the documentation for [`serde_with::StringWithSeparator::<CommaSeparator, T>`][StringWithSeparator].
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! ## Getting Help
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! **Check out the [user guide][user guide] to find out more tips and tricks about this crate.**
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! For further help using this crate you can [open a new discussion](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/discussions/new) or ask on [users.rust-lang.org](https://users.rust-lang.org/).
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! For bugs, please open a [new issue](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/issues/new) on GitHub.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! # Use `serde_with` in your Project
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! ```bash
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! # Add the current version to your Cargo.toml
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! cargo add serde_with
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! ```
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! The crate contains different features for integration with other common crates.
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! Check the [feature flags][] section for information about all available features.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! # Examples
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! Annotate your struct or enum to enable the custom de/serializer.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! The `#[serde_as]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! The `as` is analogous to the `with` attribute of serde.
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! You mirror the type structure of the field you want to de/serialize.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! You can specify converters for the inner types of a field, e.g., `Vec<DisplayFromStr>`.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! The default de/serialization behavior can be restored by using `_` as a placeholder, e.g., `BTreeMap<_, DisplayFromStr>`.
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! ## `DisplayFromStr`
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! ```rust
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! # #[cfg(all(feature = "macros", feature = "json"))] {
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! # use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! # use serde_with::{serde_as, DisplayFromStr};
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! #[serde_as]
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! # #[derive(Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! struct Foo {
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!     // Serialize with Display, deserialize with FromStr
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!     #[serde_as(as = "DisplayFromStr")]
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!     bar: u8,
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! }
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! // This will serialize
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! # let foo =
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! Foo {bar: 12}
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! # ;
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! // into this JSON
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! # let json = r#"
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! {"bar": "12"}
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! # "#;
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! # assert_eq!(json.replace(" ", "").replace("\n", ""), serde_json::to_string(&foo).unwrap());
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! # assert_eq!(foo, serde_json::from_str(json).unwrap());
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! # }
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! ```
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! ## Large and const-generic arrays
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! serde does not support arrays with more than 32 elements or using const-generics.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! The `serde_as` attribute allows circumventing this restriction, even for nested types and nested arrays.
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! On top of it, `[u8; N]` (aka, bytes) can use the specialized `"Bytes"` for efficiency much like the `serde_bytes` crate.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! ```rust
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! # #[cfg(all(feature = "macros", feature = "json"))] {
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! # use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! # use serde_with::{serde_as, Bytes};
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! #[serde_as]
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! # #[derive(Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! struct Arrays<const N: usize, const M: usize> {
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!     #[serde_as(as = "[_; N]")]
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!     constgeneric: [bool; N],
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!     #[serde_as(as = "Box<[[_; 64]; N]>")]
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!     nested: Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>,
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!     #[serde_as(as = "Option<[_; M]>")]
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!     optional: Option<[u8; M]>,
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!     #[serde_as(as = "Bytes")]
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!     bytes: [u8; M],
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! }
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! // This allows us to serialize a struct like this
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! let arrays: Arrays<100, 128> = Arrays {
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!     constgeneric: [true; 100],
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!     nested: Box::new([[111; 64]; 100]),
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!     optional: Some([222; 128]),
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!     bytes: [0x42; 128],
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! };
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! assert!(serde_json::to_string(&arrays).is_ok());
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! # }
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! ```
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! ## `skip_serializing_none`
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! This situation often occurs with JSON, but other formats also support optional fields.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! If many fields are optional, putting the annotations on the structs can become tedious.
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! The `#[skip_serializing_none]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! ```rust
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! # #[cfg(all(feature = "macros", feature = "json"))] {
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! # use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! # use serde_with::skip_serializing_none;
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! #[skip_serializing_none]
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! # #[derive(Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! struct Foo {
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!     a: Option<usize>,
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!     b: Option<usize>,
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!     c: Option<usize>,
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!     d: Option<usize>,
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!     e: Option<usize>,
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!     f: Option<usize>,
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!     g: Option<usize>,
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! }
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! // This will serialize
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! # let foo =
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! Foo {a: None, b: None, c: None, d: Some(4), e: None, f: None, g: Some(7)}
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! # ;
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! // into this JSON
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! # let json = r#"
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! {"d": 4, "g": 7}
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! # "#;
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! # assert_eq!(json.replace(" ", "").replace("\n", ""), serde_json::to_string(&foo).unwrap());
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! # assert_eq!(foo, serde_json::from_str(json).unwrap());
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! # }
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! ```
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! ## Advanced `serde_as` usage
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! This example is mainly supposed to highlight the flexibility of the `serde_as` annotation compared to [serde's `with` annotation][with-annotation].
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! More details about `serde_as` can be found in the [user guide].
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! ```rust
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! # #[cfg(all(feature = "macros", feature = "hex"))]
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! # use {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! #     serde::{Deserialize, Serialize},
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! #     serde_with::{serde_as, DisplayFromStr, DurationSeconds, hex::Hex, Map},
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! # };
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! # #[cfg(all(feature = "macros", feature = "hex"))]
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! use std::time::Duration;
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//!
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! # #[cfg(all(feature = "macros", feature = "hex"))]
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! #[serde_as]
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! # #[derive(Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! #[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! enum Foo {
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!     Durations(
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//!         // Serialize them into a list of number as seconds
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//!         #[serde_as(as = "Vec<DurationSeconds>")]
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!         Vec<Duration>,
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//!     ),
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//!     Bytes {
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!         // We can treat a Vec like a map with duplicates.
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//!         // JSON only allows string keys, so convert i32 to strings
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!         // The bytes will be hex encoded
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//!         #[serde_as(as = "Map<DisplayFromStr, Hex>")]
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//!         bytes: Vec<(i32, Vec<u8>)>,
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!     }
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! }
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! # #[cfg(all(feature = "macros", feature = "json", feature = "hex"))] {
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! // This will serialize
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! # let foo =
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! Foo::Durations(
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!     vec![Duration::new(5, 0), Duration::new(3600, 0), Duration::new(0, 0)]
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! )
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! # ;
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! // into this JSON
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! # let json = r#"
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! {
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!     "Durations": [5, 3600, 0]
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! }
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! # "#;
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! # assert_eq!(json.replace(" ", "").replace("\n", ""), serde_json::to_string(&foo).unwrap());
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! # assert_eq!(foo, serde_json::from_str(json).unwrap());
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//!
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! // and serializes
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! # let foo =
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! Foo::Bytes {
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//!     bytes: vec![
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!         (1, vec![0, 1, 2]),
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!         (-100, vec![100, 200, 255]),
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!         (1, vec![0, 111, 222]),
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!     ],
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! }
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! # ;
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! // into this JSON
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! # let json = r#"
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! {
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//!     "Bytes": {
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//!         "bytes": {
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!             "1": "000102",
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//!             "-100": "64c8ff",
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//!             "1": "006fde"
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!         }
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//!     }
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! }
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! # "#;
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! # assert_eq!(json.replace(" ", "").replace("\n", ""), serde_json::to_string(&foo).unwrap());
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! # assert_eq!(foo, serde_json::from_str(json).unwrap());
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//! # }
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! ```

[449](https://docs.rs#449)// Re-Export all proc_macros, as these should be seen as part of the serde_with crate
[450](https://docs.rs#450)#[cfg(feature = "macros")]
[451](https://docs.rs#451)#[cfg_attr(docsrs, doc(cfg(feature = "macros")))]
[452](https://docs.rs#452)#[doc(inline)]
[453](https://docs.rs#453)pub use [serde_with_macros](https://docs.rs/serde_with_macros/3.21.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_with_macros/index.html)::*;
[454](https://docs.rs#454)
[455](https://docs.rs#455)/// Adapter to convert from `serde_as` to the serde traits.
[456](https://docs.rs#456)///
[457](https://docs.rs#457)/// The `As` type adapter allows using types which implement [`DeserializeAs`] or [`SerializeAs`] in place of serde's `with` annotation.
[458](https://docs.rs#458)/// The `with` annotation allows running custom code when de/serializing, however it is quite inflexible.
[459](https://docs.rs#459)/// The traits [`DeserializeAs`]/[`SerializeAs`] are more flexible, as they allow composition and nesting of types to create more complex de/serialization behavior.
[460](https://docs.rs#460)/// However, they are not directly compatible with serde, as they are not provided by serde.
[461](https://docs.rs#461)/// The `As` type adapter makes them compatible, by forwarding the function calls to `serialize`/`deserialize` to the corresponding functions `serialize_as` and `deserialize_as`.
[462](https://docs.rs#462)///
[463](https://docs.rs#463)/// It is not required to use this type directly.
[464](https://docs.rs#464)/// Instead, it is highly encouraged to use the [`#[serde_as]`][serde_as] attribute since it includes further usability improvements.
[465](https://docs.rs#465)/// If the use of the use of the proc-macro is not acceptable, then `As` can be used directly with serde.
[466](https://docs.rs#466)///
[467](https://docs.rs#467)/// ```rust
[468](https://docs.rs#468)/// # #[cfg(feature = "alloc")] {
[469](https://docs.rs#469)/// # use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
[470](https://docs.rs#470)/// # use serde_with::{As, DisplayFromStr};
[471](https://docs.rs#471)/// #
[472](https://docs.rs#472)/// # #[allow(dead_code)]
[473](https://docs.rs#473)/// #[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
[474](https://docs.rs#474)/// # struct S {
[475](https://docs.rs#475)/// // Serialize numbers as sequence of strings, using Display and FromStr
[476](https://docs.rs#476)/// #[serde(with = "As::<Vec<DisplayFromStr>>")]
[477](https://docs.rs#477)/// field: Vec<u8>,
[478](https://docs.rs#478)/// # }
[479](https://docs.rs#479)/// # }
[480](https://docs.rs#480)/// ```
[481](https://docs.rs#481)/// If the normal `Deserialize`/`Serialize` traits should be used, the placeholder type [`Same`] can be used.
[482](https://docs.rs#482)/// It implements [`DeserializeAs`][]/[`SerializeAs`][], when the underlying type implements `Deserialize`/`Serialize`.
[483](https://docs.rs#483)///
[484](https://docs.rs#484)/// ```rust
[485](https://docs.rs#485)/// # #[cfg(feature = "alloc")] {
[486](https://docs.rs#486)/// # use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
[487](https://docs.rs#487)/// # use serde_with::{As, DisplayFromStr, Same};
[488](https://docs.rs#488)/// # use std::collections::BTreeMap;
[489](https://docs.rs#489)/// #
[490](https://docs.rs#490)/// # #[allow(dead_code)]
[491](https://docs.rs#491)/// #[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
[492](https://docs.rs#492)/// # struct S {
[493](https://docs.rs#493)/// // Serialize map, turn keys into strings but keep type of value
[494](https://docs.rs#494)/// #[serde(with = "As::<BTreeMap<DisplayFromStr, Same>>")]
[495](https://docs.rs#495)/// field: BTreeMap<u8, i32>,
[496](https://docs.rs#496)/// # }
[497](https://docs.rs#497)/// # }
[498](https://docs.rs#498)/// ```
[499](https://docs.rs#499)///
[500](https://docs.rs#500)/// [serde_as]: https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/attr.serde_as.html
[501](https://docs.rs#501)pub struct [As](https://docs.rs/serde_with/struct.As.html)<T: ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>([PhantomData](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/struct.PhantomData.html)<T>);
[502](https://docs.rs#502)
[503](https://docs.rs#503)/// Adapter to convert from `serde_as` to the serde traits.
[504](https://docs.rs#504)///
[505](https://docs.rs#505)/// This is the counter-type to [`As`][].
[506](https://docs.rs#506)/// It can be used whenever a type implementing [`DeserializeAs`]/[`SerializeAs`] is required but the normal [`Deserialize`](::serde_core::Deserialize)/[`Serialize`](::serde_core::Serialize) traits should be used.
[507](https://docs.rs#507)/// Check [`As`] for an example.
[508](https://docs.rs#508)pub struct [Same](https://docs.rs/serde_with/struct.Same.html);
[509](https://docs.rs#509)
[510](https://docs.rs#510)/// De/Serialize using [`Display`] and [`FromStr`] implementation
[511](https://docs.rs#511)///
[512](https://docs.rs#512)/// This allows deserializing a string as a number.
[513](https://docs.rs#513)/// It can be very useful for serialization formats like JSON, which do not support integer
[514](https://docs.rs#514)/// numbers and have to resort to strings to represent them.
[515](https://docs.rs#515)///
[516](https://docs.rs#516)/// Another use case is types with [`Display`] and [`FromStr`] implementations, but without serde
[517](https://docs.rs#517)/// support, which can be found in some crates.
[518](https://docs.rs#518)///
[519](https://docs.rs#519)/// If you control the type you want to de/serialize, you can instead use the two derive macros, [`SerializeDisplay`] and [`DeserializeFromStr`].
[520](https://docs.rs#520)/// They properly implement the traits [`Serialize`](::serde_core::Serialize) and [`Deserialize`](::serde_core::Deserialize) such that user of the type no longer have to use the `serde_as` system.
[521](https://docs.rs#521)///
[522](https://docs.rs#522)/// # Examples
[523](https://docs.rs#523)///
[524](https://docs.rs#524)/// ```rust
[525](https://docs.rs#525)/// # #[cfg(feature = "macros")] {
[526](https://docs.rs#526)/// # use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
[527](https://docs.rs#527)/// # use serde_json::json;
[528](https://docs.rs#528)/// # use serde_with::{serde_as, DisplayFromStr};
[529](https://docs.rs#529)/// #
[530](https://docs.rs#530)/// #[serde_as]
[531](https://docs.rs#531)/// #[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
[532](https://docs.rs#532)/// struct A {
[533](https://docs.rs#533)///     #[serde_as(as = "DisplayFromStr")]
[534](https://docs.rs#534)///     mime: mime::Mime,
[535](https://docs.rs#535)///     #[serde_as(as = "DisplayFromStr")]
[536](https://docs.rs#536)///     number: u32,
[537](https://docs.rs#537)/// }
[538](https://docs.rs#538)///
[539](https://docs.rs#539)/// let v: A = serde_json::from_value(json!({
[540](https://docs.rs#540)///     "mime": "text/plain",
[541](https://docs.rs#541)///     "number": "159",
[542](https://docs.rs#542)/// })).unwrap();
[543](https://docs.rs#543)/// assert_eq!(mime::TEXT_PLAIN, v.mime);
[544](https://docs.rs#544)/// assert_eq!(159, v.number);
[545](https://docs.rs#545)///
[546](https://docs.rs#546)/// let x = A {
[547](https://docs.rs#547)///     mime: mime::STAR_STAR,
[548](https://docs.rs#548)///     number: 777,
[549](https://docs.rs#549)/// };
[550](https://docs.rs#550)/// assert_eq!(json!({ "mime": "*/*", "number": "777" }), serde_json::to_value(x).unwrap());
[551](https://docs.rs#551)/// # }
[552](https://docs.rs#552)/// ```
[553](https://docs.rs#553)///
[554](https://docs.rs#554)/// [`Display`]: std::fmt::Display
[555](https://docs.rs#555)/// [`FromStr`]: std::str::FromStr

[558](https://docs.rs#558)/// Use the first format if [`De/Serializer::is_human_readable`], otherwise use the second
[559](https://docs.rs#559)///

[582](https://docs.rs#582)/// assert_eq!(vec![145, 205, 3, 9], rmp_serde::to_vec(&x).unwrap());
[583](https://docs.rs#583)///
[584](https://docs.rs#584)/// #[serde_as]
[585](https://docs.rs#585)/// #[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
[586](https://docs.rs#586)/// struct B {
[587](https://docs.rs#587)///     #[serde_as(as = "IfIsHumanReadable<DurationMilliSeconds, DurationSeconds>")]
[588](https://docs.rs#588)///     duration: Duration,
[589](https://docs.rs#589)/// }
[590](https://docs.rs#590)/// let x = B {
[591](https://docs.rs#591)///     duration: Duration::from_millis(1500),
[592](https://docs.rs#592)/// };
[593](https://docs.rs#593)/// assert_eq!(json!({ "duration": 1500 }), serde_json::to_value(&x).unwrap());
[594](https://docs.rs#594)/// assert_eq!(vec![145, 2], rmp_serde::to_vec(&x).unwrap());
[595](https://docs.rs#595)/// # }
[596](https://docs.rs#596)/// ```

[601](https://docs.rs#601)/// De/Serialize a [`Option<String>`] type while transforming the empty string to [`None`]
[602](https://docs.rs#602)///
[603](https://docs.rs#603)/// Convert an [`Option<T>`] from/to string using [`FromStr`] and [`Display`](::core::fmt::Display) implementations.
[604](https://docs.rs#604)/// An empty string is deserialized as [`None`] and a [`None`] vice versa.
[605](https://docs.rs#605)///
[606](https://docs.rs#606)/// # Examples
[607](https://docs.rs#607)///
[608](https://docs.rs#608)/// ```
[609](https://docs.rs#609)/// # #[cfg(feature = "macros")] {
[610](https://docs.rs#610)/// # use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
[611](https://docs.rs#611)/// # use serde_json::json;
[612](https://docs.rs#612)/// # use serde_with::{serde_as, NoneAsEmptyString};
[613](https://docs.rs#613)/// #
[614](https://docs.rs#614)/// #[serde_as]
[615](https://docs.rs#615)/// #[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
[616](https://docs.rs#616)/// struct A {
[617](https://docs.rs#617)///     #[serde_as(as = "NoneAsEmptyString")]
[618](https://docs.rs#618)///     tags: Option<String>,
[619](https://docs.rs#619)/// }
[620](https://docs.rs#620)///
[621](https://docs.rs#621)/// let v: A = serde_json::from_value(json!({ "tags": "" })).unwrap();
[622](https://docs.rs#622)/// assert_eq!(None, v.tags);
[623](https://docs.rs#623)///
[624](https://docs.rs#624)/// let v: A = serde_json::from_value(json!({ "tags": "Hi" })).unwrap();
[625](https://docs.rs#625)/// assert_eq!(Some("Hi".to_string()), v.tags);
[626](https://docs.rs#626)///
[627](https://docs.rs#627)/// let x = A {
[628](https://docs.rs#628)///     tags: Some("This is text".to_string()),
[629](https://docs.rs#629)/// };
[630](https://docs.rs#630)/// assert_eq!(json!({ "tags": "This is text" }), serde_json::to_value(x).unwrap());
[631](https://docs.rs#631)///
[632](https://docs.rs#632)/// let x = A {
[633](https://docs.rs#633)///     tags: None,
[634](https://docs.rs#634)/// };
[635](https://docs.rs#635)/// assert_eq!(json!({ "tags": "" }), serde_json::to_value(x).unwrap());
[636](https://docs.rs#636)/// # }
[637](https://docs.rs#637)/// ```
[638](https://docs.rs#638)///
[639](https://docs.rs#639)/// [`FromStr`]: std::str::FromStr
[640](https://docs.rs#640)pub struct [NoneAsEmptyString](https://docs.rs/serde_with/struct.NoneAsEmptyString.html);
[641](https://docs.rs#641)
[642](https://docs.rs#642)/// De/Serialize an [`Option<NonZero*>`] losslessly as the inner integer
[643](https://docs.rs#643)///
[644](https://docs.rs#644)/// Serde natively supports [`NonZeroU8`] and friends, but rejects `0` during deserialization.
[645](https://docs.rs#645)/// This adapter treats `0` as [`None`] and any other value as [`Some`], allowing the wire format
[646](https://docs.rs#646)/// to always be a plain integer.
[647](https://docs.rs#647)///
[648](https://docs.rs#648)/// Supported in-memory types are [`Option<NonZeroU8>`], [`Option<NonZeroU16>`], [`Option<NonZeroU32>`],
[649](https://docs.rs#649)/// [`Option<NonZeroU64>`], [`Option<NonZeroU128>`], [`Option<NonZeroUsize>`], [`Option<NonZeroI8>`],
[650](https://docs.rs#650)/// [`Option<NonZeroI16>`], [`Option<NonZeroI32>`], [`Option<NonZeroI64>`], [`Option<NonZeroI128>`],
[651](https://docs.rs#651)/// and [`Option<NonZeroIsize>`].
[652](https://docs.rs#652)///
[653](https://docs.rs#653)/// # Examples
[654](https://docs.rs#654)///
[655](https://docs.rs#655)/// ```
[656](https://docs.rs#656)/// # #[cfg(feature = "macros")] {
[657](https://docs.rs#657)/// # use core::num::NonZeroU32;
[658](https://docs.rs#658)/// # use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
[659](https://docs.rs#659)/// # use serde_json::json;
[660](https://docs.rs#660)/// # use serde_with::{serde_as, NoneAsZero};
[661](https://docs.rs#661)/// #
[662](https://docs.rs#662)/// #[serde_as]
[663](https://docs.rs#663)/// # #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
[664](https://docs.rs#664)/// #[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
[665](https://docs.rs#665)/// struct Data {
[666](https://docs.rs#666)///     #[serde_as(as = "NoneAsZero")]
[667](https://docs.rs#667)///     value: Option<NonZeroU32>,
[668](https://docs.rs#668)/// }
[669](https://docs.rs#669)///
[670](https://docs.rs#670)/// let data = Data { value: NonZeroU32::new(7) };
[671](https://docs.rs#671)/// assert_eq!(json!({"value": 7}), serde_json::to_value(&data).unwrap());
[672](https://docs.rs#672)/// assert_eq!(data, serde_json::from_value(json!({"value": 7})).unwrap());
[673](https://docs.rs#673)///
[674](https://docs.rs#674)/// let none = Data { value: None };
[675](https://docs.rs#675)/// assert_eq!(json!({"value": 0}), serde_json::to_value(&none).unwrap());
[676](https://docs.rs#676)/// assert_eq!(none, serde_json::from_value(json!({"value": 0})).unwrap());
[677](https://docs.rs#677)/// # }
[678](https://docs.rs#678)/// ```
[679](https://docs.rs#679)///
[680](https://docs.rs#680)/// [`NonZeroU8`]: core::num::NonZeroU8
[681](https://docs.rs#681)/// [`Option<NonZeroU8>`]: core::num::NonZeroU8
[682](https://docs.rs#682)/// [`Option<NonZeroU16>`]: core::num::NonZeroU16
[683](https://docs.rs#683)/// [`Option<NonZeroU32>`]: core::num::NonZeroU32
[684](https://docs.rs#684)/// [`Option<NonZeroU64>`]: core::num::NonZeroU64
[685](https://docs.rs#685)/// [`Option<NonZeroU128>`]: core::num::NonZeroU128
[686](https://docs.rs#686)/// [`Option<NonZeroUsize>`]: core::num::NonZeroUsize
[687](https://docs.rs#687)/// [`Option<NonZeroI8>`]: core::num::NonZeroI8
[688](https://docs.rs#688)/// [`Option<NonZeroI16>`]: core::num::NonZeroI16
[689](https://docs.rs#689)/// [`Option<NonZeroI32>`]: core::num::NonZeroI32
[690](https://docs.rs#690)/// [`Option<NonZeroI64>`]: core::num::NonZeroI64
[691](https://docs.rs#691)/// [`Option<NonZeroI128>`]: core::num::NonZeroI128
[692](https://docs.rs#692)/// [`Option<NonZeroIsize>`]: core::num::NonZeroIsize
[693](https://docs.rs#693)pub struct [NoneAsZero](https://docs.rs/serde_with/struct.NoneAsZero.html);
[694](https://docs.rs#694)
[695](https://docs.rs#695)/// Deserialize value and return [`Default`] on error
[696](https://docs.rs#696)///
[697](https://docs.rs#697)/// The main use case is ignoring error while deserializing.
[698](https://docs.rs#698)/// Instead of erroring, it simply deserializes the [`Default`] variant of the type.
[699](https://docs.rs#699)/// It is not possible to find the error location, i.e., which field had a deserialization error, with this method.
[700](https://docs.rs#700)/// During serialization this wrapper does nothing.
[701](https://docs.rs#701)/// The serialization behavior of the underlying type is preserved.
[702](https://docs.rs#702)/// The type must implement [`Default`] for this conversion to work.
[703](https://docs.rs#703)///
[704](https://docs.rs#704)/// # Examples
[705](https://docs.rs#705)///
[706](https://docs.rs#706)/// ```
[707](https://docs.rs#707)/// # #[cfg(feature = "macros")] {
[708](https://docs.rs#708)/// # use serde::Deserialize;
[709](https://docs.rs#709)/// # use serde_with::{serde_as, DefaultOnError};
[710](https://docs.rs#710)/// #
[711](https://docs.rs#711)/// #[serde_as]
[712](https://docs.rs#712)/// #[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
[713](https://docs.rs#713)/// struct A {
[714](https://docs.rs#714)///     #[serde_as(deserialize_as = "DefaultOnError")]
[715](https://docs.rs#715)///     value: u32,
[716](https://docs.rs#716)/// }
[717](https://docs.rs#717)///
[718](https://docs.rs#718)/// let a: A = serde_json::from_str(r#"{"value": 123}"#).unwrap();
[719](https://docs.rs#719)/// assert_eq!(123, a.value);
[720](https://docs.rs#720)///
[721](https://docs.rs#721)/// // null is of invalid type
[722](https://docs.rs#722)/// let a: A = serde_json::from_str(r#"{"value": null}"#).unwrap();
[723](https://docs.rs#723)/// assert_eq!(0, a.value);
[724](https://docs.rs#724)///
[725](https://docs.rs#725)/// // String is of invalid type
[726](https://docs.rs#726)/// let a: A = serde_json::from_str(r#"{"value": "123"}"#).unwrap();
[727](https://docs.rs#727)/// assert_eq!(0, a.value);
[728](https://docs.rs#728)///
[729](https://docs.rs#729)/// // Map is of invalid type
[730](https://docs.rs#730)/// let a: A = dbg!(serde_json::from_str(r#"{"value": {}}"#)).unwrap();
[731](https://docs.rs#731)/// assert_eq!(0, a.value);
[732](https://docs.rs#732)///
[733](https://docs.rs#733)/// // Missing entries still cause errors
[734](https://docs.rs#734)/// assert!(serde_json::from_str::<A>(r#"{  }"#).is_err());
[735](https://docs.rs#735)/// # }
[736](https://docs.rs#736)/// ```
[737](https://docs.rs#737)///
[738](https://docs.rs#738)/// Deserializing missing values can be supported by adding the `default` field attribute:
[739](https://docs.rs#739)///
[740](https://docs.rs#740)/// ```
[741](https://docs.rs#741)/// # #[cfg(feature = "macros")] {
[742](https://docs.rs#742)/// # use serde::Deserialize;
[743](https://docs.rs#743)/// # use serde_with::{serde_as, DefaultOnError};
[744](https://docs.rs#744)/// #
[745](https://docs.rs#745)/// #[serde_as]
[746](https://docs.rs#746)/// #[derive(Deserialize)]
[747](https://docs.rs#747)/// struct B {
[748](https://docs.rs#748)///     #[serde_as(deserialize_as = "DefaultOnError")]
[749](https://docs.rs#749)///     #[serde(default)]
[750](https://docs.rs#750)///     value: u32,
[751](https://docs.rs#751)/// }
[752](https://docs.rs#752)///
[753](https://docs.rs#753)/// let b: B = serde_json::from_str(r#"{  }"#).unwrap();
[754](https://docs.rs#754)/// assert_eq!(0, b.value);
[755](https://docs.rs#755)/// # }
[756](https://docs.rs#756)/// ```
[757](https://docs.rs#757)///
[758](https://docs.rs#758)/// `DefaultOnError` can be combined with other conversion methods.
[759](https://docs.rs#759)/// In this example, we deserialize a `Vec`, each element is deserialized from a string.
[760](https://docs.rs#760)/// If the string does not parse as a number, then we get the default value of 0.
[761](https://docs.rs#761)///
[762](https://docs.rs#762)/// ```rust
[763](https://docs.rs#763)/// # #[cfg(feature = "macros")] {
[764](https://docs.rs#764)/// # use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
[765](https://docs.rs#765)/// # use serde_json::json;
[766](https://docs.rs#766)/// # use serde_with::{serde_as, DefaultOnError, DisplayFromStr};
[767](https://docs.rs#767)/// #
[768](https://docs.rs#768)/// #[serde_as]
[769](https://docs.rs#769)/// #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
[770](https://docs.rs#770)/// struct C {
[771](https://docs.rs#771)///     #[serde_as(as = "Vec<DefaultOnError<DisplayFromStr>>")]
[772](https://docs.rs#772)///     value: Vec<u32>,
[773](https://docs.rs#773)/// }
[774](https://docs.rs#774)///
[775](https://docs.rs#775)/// let c: C = serde_json::from_value(json!({
[776](https://docs.rs#776)///     "value": ["1", "2", "a3", "", {}, "6"]
[777](https://docs.rs#777)/// })).unwrap();
[778](https://docs.rs#778)/// assert_eq!(vec![1, 2, 0, 0, 0, 6], c.value);
[779](https://docs.rs#779)/// # }
[780](https://docs.rs#780)/// ```
[781](https://docs.rs#781)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[782](https://docs.rs#782)pub struct [DefaultOnError](https://docs.rs/serde_with/struct.DefaultOnError.html)<T = [Same](https://docs.rs#508)>([PhantomData](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/struct.PhantomData.html)<T>);
[783](https://docs.rs#783)
[784](https://docs.rs#784)/// Deserialize [`Default`] from `null` values
[785](https://docs.rs#785)///
[786](https://docs.rs#786)/// Instead of erroring on `null` values, it simply deserializes the [`Default`] variant of the type.
[787](https://docs.rs#787)/// During serialization this wrapper does nothing.
[788](https://docs.rs#788)/// The serialization behavior of the underlying type is preserved.
[789](https://docs.rs#789)/// The type must implement [`Default`] for this conversion to work.
[790](https://docs.rs#790)///
[791](https://docs.rs#791)/// # Examples
[792](https://docs.rs#792)///
[793](https://docs.rs#793)/// ```
[794](https://docs.rs#794)/// # #[cfg(feature = "macros")] {
[795](https://docs.rs#795)/// # use serde::Deserialize;
[796](https://docs.rs#796)/// # use serde_with::{serde_as, DefaultOnNull};
[797](https://docs.rs#797)/// #
[798](https://docs.rs#798)/// #[serde_as]
[799](https://docs.rs#799)/// #[derive(Deserialize, Debug)]
[800](https://docs.rs#800)/// struct A {
[801](https://docs.rs#801)///     #[serde_as(deserialize_as = "DefaultOnNull")]
[802](https://docs.rs#802)///     value: u32,
[803](https://docs.rs#803)/// }
[804](https://docs.rs#804)///
[805](https://docs.rs#805)/// let a: A = serde_json::from_str(r#"{"value": 123}"#).unwrap();
[806](https://docs.rs#806)/// assert_eq!(123, a.value);
[807](https://docs.rs#807)///
[808](https://docs.rs#808)/// // null values are deserialized into the default, here 0
[809](https://docs.rs#809)/// let a: A = serde_json::from_str(r#"{"value": null}"#).unwrap();
[810](https://docs.rs#810)/// assert_eq!(0, a.value);
[811](https://docs.rs#811)/// # }
[812](https://docs.rs#812)/// ```
[813](https://docs.rs#813)///
[814](https://docs.rs#814)/// `DefaultOnNull` can be combined with other conversion methods.
[815](https://docs.rs#815)/// In this example, we deserialize a `Vec`, each element is deserialized from a string.
[816](https://docs.rs#816)/// If we encounter null, then we get the default value of 0.
[817](https://docs.rs#817)///
[818](https://docs.rs#818)/// ```rust
[819](https://docs.rs#819)/// # #[cfg(feature = "macros")] {
[820](https://docs.rs#820)/// # use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
[821](https://docs.rs#821)/// # use serde_json::json;
[822](https://docs.rs#822)/// # use serde_with::{serde_as, DefaultOnNull, DisplayFromStr};
[823](https://docs.rs#823)/// #
[824](https://docs.rs#824)/// #[serde_as]
[825](https://docs.rs#825)/// #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
[826](https://docs.rs#826)/// struct C {
[827](https://docs.rs#827)///     #[serde_as(as = "Vec<DefaultOnNull<DisplayFromStr>>")]
[828](https://docs.rs#828)///     value: Vec<u32>,
[829](https://docs.rs#829)/// }
[830](https://docs.rs#830)///
[831](https://docs.rs#831)/// let c: C = serde_json::from_value(json!({
[832](https://docs.rs#832)///     "value": ["1", "2", null, null, "5"]
[833](https://docs.rs#833)/// })).unwrap();
[834](https://docs.rs#834)/// assert_eq!(vec![1, 2, 0, 0, 5], c.value);
[835](https://docs.rs#835)/// # }
[836](https://docs.rs#836)/// ```
[837](https://docs.rs#837)pub struct [DefaultOnNull](https://docs.rs/serde_with/struct.DefaultOnNull.html)<T = [Same](https://docs.rs#508)>([PhantomData](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/marker/struct.PhantomData.html)<T>);
[838](https://docs.rs#838)
[839](https://docs.rs#839)/// Deserialize from bytes or string
[840](https://docs.rs#840)///
[841](https://docs.rs#841)/// Any Rust [`String`] can be converted into bytes, i.e., `Vec<u8>`.
[842](https://docs.rs#842)/// Accepting both as formats while deserializing can be helpful while interacting with language
[843](https://docs.rs#843)/// which have a looser definition of string than Rust.
[844](https://docs.rs#844)///
[845](https://docs.rs#845)/// # Example
[846](https://docs.rs#846)/// ```rust
[847](https://docs.rs#847)/// # #[cfg(feature = "macros")] {
[848](https://docs.rs#848)/// # use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
[849](https://docs.rs#849)/// # use serde_json::json;
[850](https://docs.rs#850)/// # use serde_with::{serde_as, BytesOrString};
[851](https://docs.rs#851)/// #
[852](https://docs.rs#852)/// #[serde_as]
[853](https://docs.rs#853)/// #[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
[854](https://docs.rs#854)/// struct A {
[855](https://docs.rs#855)///     #[serde_as(as = "BytesOrString")]
[856](https://docs.rs#856)///     bytes_or_string: Vec<u8>,
[857](https://docs.rs#857)/// }
[858](https://docs.rs#858)///
[859](https://docs.rs#859)/// // Here we deserialize from a byte array ...
[860](https://docs.rs#860)/// let j = json!({
[861](https://docs.rs#861)///   "bytes_or_string": [
[862](https://docs.rs#862)///     0,
[863](https://docs.rs#863)///     1,
[864](https://docs.rs#864)///     2,
[865](https://docs.rs#865)///     3
[866](https://docs.rs#866)///   ]
[867](https://docs.rs#867)/// });
[868](https://docs.rs#868)///
[869](https://docs.rs#869)/// let a: A = serde_json::from_value(j.clone()).unwrap();
[870](https://docs.rs#870)/// assert_eq!(vec![0, 1, 2, 3], a.bytes_or_string);
[871](https://docs.rs#871)///
[872](https://docs.rs#872)/// // and serialization works too.
[873](https://docs.rs#873)/// assert_eq!(j, serde_json::to_value(&a).unwrap());
[874](https://docs.rs#874)///
[875](https://docs.rs#875)/// // But we also support deserializing from a String
[876](https://docs.rs#876)/// let j = json!({
[877](https://docs.rs#877)///   "bytes_or_string": "✨Works!"
[878](https://docs.rs#878)/// });
[879](https://docs.rs#879)///
